analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal aid to colleges whose graduates can't repay loans and makes colleges share the cost.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill that would cut off federal student aid to colleges where few borrowers pay down their loans was referred to the education committee in March 2026 and has not moved since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut off a college's access to federal student aid for three years if 15% or fewer of its borrowers pay down even one dollar of loan principal within two years of entering repayment. Colleges whose borrowers don't repay would also owe the Education Department a 'risk-sharing' payment of 2% of the unpaid loan balances (capped at 2.5% of the school's annual revenues), and those payments would fund grants to colleges with strong records helping low- and moderate-income students. It would also require colleges to report how much they spend on student services versus on marketing and recruiting.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and families, chiefly at schools with poor loan outcomes: a school that keeps loading students with debt they can't repay would lose federal aid eligibility, and colleges that successfully serve low-income students would get new grant money for need-based aid and support services. Taxpayers also gain, since colleges would share the cost of loans that never get repaid instead of the Department of Education absorbing the full loss.

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in fiscal year 2028, a college where 15% or fewer of borrowers make at least a one-dollar reduction on their loan principal within two years of entering repayment loses eligibility for federal student aid programs for three years, with an appeals process.

Colleges with borrowers who don't repay would owe the Department a risk-sharing payment equal to 2% of the cohort's nonrepaid loan balance, adjusted for the national unemployment rate and capped at 2.5% of the institution's annual revenues.

Those risk-sharing payments would fund a new grant program for colleges with repayment rates above 25% and a strong record with low- and moderate-income students, usable for extra need-based aid, academic and student support services, and accelerated learning opportunities.

The repayment metric excludes borrowers in legitimate deferment — graduate school, at least half-time enrollment, military service, disability rehabilitation, mandatory forbearance, and Peace Corps service — so students who are still in school or serving are not counted against their school.

The National Center for Education Statistics would have to collect data separating spending on student services from spending on recruitment and marketing, making it easier to see whether a college is spending on students or on filling seats.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities whose borrowers don't repay their loans — most heavily for-profit colleges, where weak repayment rates are concentrated, but also any institution whose graduates struggle to pay down principal. Institutions that lose federal aid eligibility would see students unable to use grants and loans there, and schools facing risk-sharing payments could pass costs to students through tuition or cut aid.

drawbacks.text: The repayment measure counts only principal reduction. Borrowers who stay current on income-driven repayment plans often pay interest without reducing principal, so a borrower who is paying as required could still count against their school — and a school cut off from federal aid would leave its enrolled students with no access to Pell Grants or federal loans.

Repayment rates track graduates' incomes, not just school quality, so colleges serving the lowest-income students — community colleges, Historically Black Colleges and Universities, and other broad-access schools — are the most likely to be caught even when their students get real value. The bill acknowledges this by requiring a report on how such institutions can improve repayment rates.
The new grant program is only open to colleges with repayment rates above 25%, which can exclude the very broad-access institutions that enroll the most low-income students.
Risk-sharing payments could be passed on to students as higher tuition or reduced institutional aid, since the obligation falls on the college, not the state or the borrower.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — making colleges bear some cost when students leave with debt they cannot pay down — addresses a real and expensive failure that today costs taxpayers and traps borrowers. The design guards against some unfairness by excluding borrowers in school, in the military, or in deferment, and by adjusting payments for unemployment. But tying consequences to principal repayment rather than to default or income is a blunt instrument: it can punish colleges for whom their students are, not what they teach them, and a three-year total aid cutoff would punish enrolled students hardest. A fairer version would use a softer escalation before cutting schools off entirely.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen introduced the Student Protection and Success Act in the Senate on March 17, 2026, joined by Sen. Todd Young, making it a two-sponsor bipartisan bill.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has been affected because nothing has happened. If the bill stays parked, colleges with weak repayment outcomes keep full access to federal aid and taxpayers keep absorbing the losses on loans those students can't repay. Enrolled students at the worst-performing schools also avoid the risk of losing aid access if their school were cut off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Colleges with weak outcomes, so far

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only demonstrated support is bipartisan — one Democrat and one Republican — but with no votes yet there is no record of where the wider chambers stand.

industries.note: Weak repayment rates are concentrated in this sector, so the three-year aid cutoff and risk-sharing payments fall hardest here. The industry profits from federal loans students cannot repay, so its interest in stopping the bill runs against borrowers and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Community colleges and other broad-access public institutions
industries.note: Risk-sharing payments apply to any college whose borrowers don't pay down principal, and these schools serve many low-income students whose repayment lags for income reasons. They are also the schools the bill's grant program is least likely to reach, since eligibility requires a repayment rate above 25%.

Schools with strong repayment rates could gain grant money for low-income students; schools with weak rates owe risk-sharing payments up to 2.5% of annual revenues. All would face new public reporting of what they spend on marketing and recruiting versus student services.
The federal government currently absorbs most losses on student loans that go unpaid; risk-sharing shifts part of that cost to the colleges that enrolled the borrowers.

analysis.trajectory: With the 119th Congress ending January 3, 2027 and no committee action since the March 2026 referral, a standalone vote is unlikely. The bill's realistic path is being folded into broader Higher Education Act reauthorization negotiations, where repayment-based accountability is an active topic; otherwise it will die quietly at the end of the Congress.
